claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Luger et al., 1997, which provides established knowledge about nucleosome structure.

claims.claim: H3K36 di- and tri-methylation (H3K36me2/3) are enriched in coding regions and toward the 3' end of actively transcribed genes.
claims.source: In contrast with many PTMs whose spatial distribution is skewed towards promoters and the 5' regions of genes, H3K36 di- and tri-methylation (H3K36me2/3) are enriched in coding regions and toward the 3' end of actively transcribed genes (Bannister et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bannister et al., 2005, which provides published evidence for the distribution of H3K36me2/3.

claims.claim: H3K36me2/3 marks are preferentially enriched over exons as opposed to introns.
claims.source: These marks are also preferentially enriched over exons as opposed to introns (Kolasinska-Zwierz et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kolasinska-Zwierz et al., 2009, which provides published evidence for the exonic enrichment of H3K36me2/3.

claims.claim: H3K36me3 suppresses cryptic transcription initiation from coding regions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae by recruiting a repressive Rpd3 deacetylase complex to sites of active elongation.
claims.source: Indeed, H3K36me2/3 is known to suppress cryptic transcription initiation from coding regions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae by recruiting a repressive Rpd3 deacetylase complex to sites of active elongation (Carrozza et al., 2005; Keogh et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carrozza et al., 2005 and Keogh et al., 2005, which provide published evidence for this mechanism in yeast.

claims.claim: H3K36me3 is implicated in suppressing active incorporation of acetylated histones via histone exchange.
claims.source: It is also implicated in suppressing active incorporation of acetylated histones via histone exchange (Venkatesh et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Venkatesh et al., 2012, which provides published evidence for this mechanism.

claims.claim: Ablation of human SETD2 is suggested to alter a number of exon inclusion events by recruiting RNA binding proteins in cultured cells.
claims.source: In cultured cells, ablation of human SETD2, which catalyzes H3K36 trimethylation, is suggested to alter a number of exon inclusion events by recruiting RNA binding proteins (Luco et al., 2010; Pradeepa et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Luco et al., 2010 and Pradeepa et al., 2012, which provide published evidence for this role of SETD2.

claims.claim: H3K36me3 distribution across gene bodies is sensitive to perturbations in splicing.
claims.source: Conversely, H3K36me3 distribution across gene bodies is itself sensitive to perturbations in splicing (de Almeida et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Almeida et al., 2011 and Kim et al., 2011, which provide published evidence for this relationship.

claims.claim: H3K36me has been attributed roles in X-chromosome dosage compensation.
claims.source: In addition to its role in transcription and RNA processing, a range of other activities have been attributed to H3K36me, including X-chromosome dosage compensation (Larschan et al., 2007), DNA damage response (Jha and Strahl, 2014; Li et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2014; Pfister et al., 2014), and three dimensional chromosome organization (Evans et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2013; Ulianov et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Larschan et al., 2007, which provides published evidence for this role.

claims.claim: H3K36me has been attributed roles in DNA damage response.
claims.source: In addition to its role in transcription and RNA processing, a range of other activities have been attributed to H3K36me, including X-chromosome dosage compensation (Larschan et al., 2007), DNA damage response (Jha and Strahl, 2014; Li et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2014; Pfister et al., 2014), and three dimensional chromosome organization (Evans et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2013; Ulianov et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jha and Strahl, 2014; Li et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2014; and Pfister et al., 2014, which provide published evidence for this role.

claims.claim: H3K36me has been attributed roles in three dimensional chromosome organization.
claims.source: In addition to its role in transcription and RNA processing, a range of other activities have been attributed to H3K36me, including X-chromosome dosage compensation (Larschan et al., 2007), DNA damage response (Jha and Strahl, 2014; Li et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2014; Pfister et al., 2014), and three dimensional chromosome organization (Evans et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2013; Ulianov et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Evans et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2013; and Ulianov et al., 2016, which provide published evidence for this role.

claims.claim: Arginine approximates the charge and steric conformation of lysine.
claims.source: Arginine approximates the charge and steric conformation of lysine, but cannot be targeted by lysine methyltransferases, and therefore represents an appropriate mutation with which to study the PTM-specific functions of H3K36.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of amino acid properties.

claims.claim: Arginine cannot be targeted by lysine methyltransferases.
claims.source: Arginine approximates the charge and steric conformation of lysine, but cannot be targeted by lysine methyltransferases, and therefore represents an appropriate mutation with which to study the PTM-specific functions of H3K36.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of enzyme specificity.

claims.claim: H3K36me3 is catalyzed co-transcriptionally.
claims.source: Because H3K36me3 is catalyzed co-transcriptionally (Kizer et al., 2005), and should therefore track roughly with gene expression, we also took the alternate approach of determining whether gene expression changes in K36R were correlated with the amount of expression normally observed in HWT.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kizer et al., 2005, which provides published evidence for co-transcriptional catalysis of H3K36me3.

claims.claim: SETD2 catalyzes trimethylation of lysine 36 in both the 'canonical' replication-dependent H3 and in the replication-independent histone variant, H3.3.
claims.source: Perhaps more importantly, SETD2 catalyzes trimethylation of lysine 36 in both the 'canonical' replication-dependent H3 and in the replication-independent histone variant, H3.3.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of SETD2 substrate specificity.

claims.claim: H3.3 is thought to play a particularly important role in transcriptionally active regions where H3K36 methylation is enriched.
claims.source: H3.3 is thought to play a particularly important role in transcriptionally active regions where H3K36 methylation is enriched (Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002, which provides published evidence for the role of H3.3 in transcriptionally active regions.

claims.claim: A protein with specific affinity for SETD2-catalyzed trimethylation of lysine 36 of the histone H3.3 variant serves as a regulator of RNA pol II elongation.
claims.source: Indeed, a protein with specific affinity for SETD2-catalyzed trimethylation of lysine 36 of the histone H3.3 variant was shown to serve as a regulator of RNA pol II elongation (Wen et al., 2014) and to associate with components of spliceosomal snRNPs to regulate co-transcriptional alternative mRNA splicing (Guo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wen et al., 2014, which provides published evidence for this regulatory role.

claims.claim: A protein with specific affinity for SETD2-catalyzed trimethylation of lysine 36 of the histone H3.3 variant associates with components of spliceosomal snRNPs to regulate co-transcriptional alternative mRNA splicing.
claims.source: Indeed, a protein with specific affinity for SETD2-catalyzed trimethylation of lysine 36 of the histone H3.3 variant was shown to serve as a regulator of RNA pol II elongation (Wen et al., 2014) and to associate with components of spliceosomal snRNPs to regulate co-transcriptional alternative mRNA splicing (Guo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2014, which provides published evidence for this regulatory role.

claims.claim: SETD2's prominent association with the C-terminal domain of RNA pol II makes it likely that ablating this protein will result in transcriptional consequences that are unrelated to its catalytic activity.
claims.source: Beyond its other substrates, SETD2's prominent association with the C-terminal domain of RNA pol II (Kizer et al., 2005) makes it likely that ablating this protein will result in transcriptional consequences that are unrelated to its catalytic activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the known association of SETD2 with RNA pol II, supported by citation to Kizer et al., 2005, and represents speculation about the consequences of SETD2 ablation.

claims.claim: H3K36me3 depletion in SETD2-mutant renal cell carcinoma has been correlated with defects in transcriptional termination and readthrough into neighboring genes.
claims.source: Interestingly, H3K36me3 depletion in SETD2-mutant renal cell carcinoma has been correlated with defects in transcriptional termination and readthrough into neighboring genes (Grosso et al., 2015), suggesting that H3K36 methylation might influence termination and polyadenylation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grosso et al., 2015, which provides published evidence for this correlation.

claims.claim: Dimethylation (N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine, or m6Am) of the nucleotide adjacent to the m7G cap enhances transcript stability.
claims.source: For example, Jaffrey and colleagues recently showed that dimethylation (N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine, or m6Am) of the nucleotide adjacent to the m7G cap enhances transcript stability (Mauer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mauer et al., 2017, which provides published evidence for this mechanism.

claims.claim: The prevailing model for histone PTM modulation of gene expression suggests that it occurs directly proximal to the site of histone modification.
claims.source: The prevailing model for histone PTM modulation of gene expression, reinforced by recent direct evidence (Hilton et al., 2015), suggests that it occurs directly proximal to the site of histone modification.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hilton et al., 2015, which provides published evidence for this model.

claims.claim: Alpha-tubulin was recently identified as a non-histone substrate of SETD2.
claims.source: Notably, alpha-tubulin was recently identified as a non-histone substrate of SETD2 (Park et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Park et al., 2016, which provides published evidence for this substrate identification.

claims.claim: Very low levels of H3K36me3 signal are observed in both western blots from H3K36R mutant larvae and immunofluorescent staining of salivary gland polytene chromosomes.
claims.source: However, this possibility should be tempered by the fact that we observed very low levels of H3K36me3 signal in both western blots from H3K36R mutant larvae (Figure 3A) and immunofluorescent staining of salivary gland polytene chromosomes (McKay et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 3A and citation to McKay et al., 2015 for immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: H3.3 is, at best, a minor contributor to total H3K36me3.
claims.source: Thus H3.3 is, at best, a minor contributor to total H3K36me3.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that very low levels of H3K36me3 remain in H3K36R mutants where only H3.3 could be methylated.

claims.claim: Start-seq signal maps faithfully and robustly, with base-pair resolution, to annotated (observed) transcription start sites (obsTSSs).
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C, Start-seq signal maps faithfully and robustly, with base-pair resolution, to annotated (observed) transcription start sites (obsTSSs), and demarcates sites of high nuclear RNA-seq.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the Start-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C.

claims.claim: Start-seq demarcates sites of high nuclear RNA-seq.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C, Start-seq signal maps faithfully and robustly, with base-pair resolution, to annotated (observed) transcription start sites (obsTSSs), and demarcates sites of high nuclear RNA-seq.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of Start-seq and nuclear RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C.

claims.claim: ATAC-seq signal accumulates most robustly in a window spanning roughly 150 nt upstream, and 50 nt downstream, of obsTSSs.
claims.source: ATAC-seq signal accumulates most robustly in a window spanning roughly 150 nt upstream, and 50 nt downstream, of obsTSSs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: Exonic nuTSSs are depleted of ATAC-seq open chromatin signal.
claims.source: Similarly, exonic nuTSSs are depleted of ATAC-seq open chromatin signal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The findings do not support a role in Drosophila for H3K36me in suppressing cryptic antisense transcription, as described in yeast.
claims.source: Importantly, these findings do not support a role in Drosophila for H3K36me in suppressing cryptic antisense transcription, as described in yeast.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that antisense transcription does not increase in K36R mutants, in contrast to what has been observed in yeast.

claims.claim: The SETD2 methyltransferase is reported to play a role in regulating alternative splice site choice.
claims.source: The H3K36me3 methyltransferase, SETD2, is reported to play a role in regulating alternative splice site choice (Luco et al., 2010; Pradeepa et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Luco et al., 2010 and Pradeepa et al., 2012, which provide published evidence for this role.

claims.claim: Studies have implicated H3K36me3 in inefficient intron splicing in clear cell renal cell carcinomas via SETD2 mutation.
claims.source: Furthermore, studies have implicated H3K36me3 in alternative splicing in human cell culture (Luco et al., 2010; Pradeepa et al., 2012) and inefficient intron splicing in clear cell renal cell carcinomas (Simon et al., 2014), again via SETD2 mutation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Simon et al., 2014, which provides published evidence for this role.

claims.claim: H3K36 is neither a significant contributor to the regulation of alternative splice site choice, nor the efficiency of canonical intron removal.
claims.source: We demonstrate that H3K36 is neither a significant contributor to the regulation of alternative splice site choice, nor the efficiency of canonical intron removal.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the MISO and splice junction analysis presented in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Methylation of H3K36 does not suppress cryptic transcription in coding regions.
claims.source: We also present evidence that methylation of H3K36 does not suppress cryptic transcription in coding regions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the Start-seq analysis presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: H4 acetylation is strongly suppressed by H3K36 modification.

claims.claim: Cryptic transcripts do not appear in H3K36R mutants despite increased H4 acetylation.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the Start-seq analysis shown in Figure 4 combined with the western blot data in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The finding argues for an uncoupling of H4ac levels from cryptic initiation in coding regions in metazoans.
claims.source: This finding argues for an uncoupling of H4ac levels from cryptic initiation in coding regions in metazoans, and suggests that the suppression of cryptic transcription initiation in multicellular organisms may be more complex than previously appreciated.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that H4 acetylation increases in K36R mutants without a corresponding increase in cryptic transcription.

claims.claim: The suppression of cryptic transcription initiation in multicellular organisms may be more complex than previously appreciated.

claims.evidence: This claim represents speculation based on the unexpected finding that H4 hyperacetylation does not lead to cryptic transcription in Drosophila.

claims.claim: H3K36 is required for proper mRNA maturation, providing a post-transcriptional benefit across a range of highly expressed genes.
claims.source: Finally, we present evidence that H3K36 is required for proper mRNA maturation, providing a post-transcriptional benefit across a range of highly expressed genes.

results.result: H3K36R mutants exhibit severe developmental defects including reduced pupation frequency and complete failure to eclose into adults, without obvious cell proliferation defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are all supported by citation to McKay et al., 2015, representing prior published work. These phenotypic observations establish the biological context for the current study and are appropriately attributed to previous research.

results.result: H3K36R mutation causes widespread transcriptome dysregulation where genes with high H3K36me3 density decrease expression while genes with low H3K36me3 density increase expression, with the strongest effects in highly expressed and lowly expressed genes respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C10 are well-supported by poly-A RNA-seq data shown in Figures 2A-C. The anticorrelation between H3K36me3 density and gene expression changes is demonstrated across multiple analyses. The global nature of effects argues against an exclusively local, cis-acting mechanism.

results.result: H3K36R mutants exhibit robustly increased H4 acetylation levels, particularly in transcriptionally active regions, while H3K27me3 levels are slightly reduced but polycomb target genes remain largely unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C15 and C80 are supported by western blot data (Figure 3A), immunofluorescence on polytene chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), and gene expression analysis. The H4 hyperacetylation confirms the previously identified link between H3K36me and H4ac, while the minimal effect on polycomb targets is appropriately documented.

results.result: Global chromatin accessibility at promoters is minimally changed between HWT and H3K36R animals, indicating that chromatin remodeling at promoters is not a major contributor to observed gene expression changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C16 and C18 are supported by ATAC-seq data (Figure 3B) showing high correlation between HWT and K36R at transcription start sites, and by the lack of correlation between ATAC-seq changes and differential expression (Figure 3C). This argues against a promoter-centric mechanism.

results.result: Contrary to expectations from yeast studies, H3K36 methylation does not suppress cryptic transcription in Drosophila gene bodies. Instead, pervasive initiation is widespread throughout the genome even in wild-type animals, and exonic/antisense transcription does not increase in K36R mutants despite H4 hyperacetylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C27, C75, C79, C81-C82 are well-supported by extensive Start-seq analysis (>200M reads, Figure 4). The identification of thousands of nuTSSs in wild-type, the lack of increased cryptic transcription in K36R mutants, and the uncoupling of H4 acetylation from cryptic initiation represent major findings that challenge the prevailing model from yeast. The depth of sequencing provides strong statistical power.

results.result: H3K36 mutation has minimal effects on alternative splicing, with very few differential splicing events detected and no changes in global splice junction usage, indicating that H3K36 is not a significant contributor to splicing regulation in Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 and C78 are supported by comprehensive MISO analysis (Figure 5A-B) and global splice junction analysis (Figure 5C). The findings contradict previous reports based on SETD2 depletion, suggesting those effects may be due to non-histone functions of SETD2. The statistical criteria for significance are clearly defined.

results.result: A subset of highly expressed genes shows reduced transcript levels in poly-A RNA but not nuclear RNA in K36R mutants. This defect is rescued by RNAi depletion of the exonuclease pacman and deadenylases twin and Pop2, but not by Dcp2 depletion, indicating H3K36 contributes to post-transcriptional mRNA maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 and C84 are supported by comparison of poly-A and nuclear RNA-seq (Figure 6A-B), RT-PCR fractionation experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and RT-qPCR rescue experiments (Figure 6C). The selective rescue by specific RNA degradation factors provides mechanistic insight. However, the Dcp2 result is acknowledged as inconclusive due to known redundancies.

results.result: H3K36R mutants exhibit reduced poly-A tail length that is independent of deadenylation activity, indicating a defect in polyadenylation rather than subsequent deadenylation. Poly-A site specification remains largely unaffected, suggesting H3K36 has a post-transcriptional role in mRNA maturation linked to 3' end formation efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 and C85 are supported by LM-PAT assay data (Figure 6D) showing reduced poly-A tail length in K36R that persists even with deadenylase depletion, and DaPars analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) showing no change in poly-A site usage. The YFP reporter provides a controlled system, though transcriptome-wide validation is noted as needed.

results.result: Very low levels of H3K36me3 signal remain in H3K36R mutants, indicating that the histone variant H3.3 is at best a minor contributor to total H3K36me3.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are supported by western blot data (Figure 3A) and citation to immunofluorescence data from McKay et al., 2015. This observation is important for interpreting the results, as it suggests the phenotypes observed are primarily due to loss of canonical H3K36 methylation rather than H3.3K36 methylation.

results.result: Start-seq signal maps faithfully to annotated transcription start sites with base-pair resolution and correlates with nuclear RNA-seq signal. ATAC-seq signal accumulates in a defined window around TSSs, with exonic nuTSSs depleted of open chromatin signal.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 are supported by validation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A. These technical validation results establish the quality and reliability of the sequencing methods used, which is essential for interpreting the biological findings.

results.result: Background claims establishing prior knowledge about chromatin structure, H3K36 methylation distribution and functions, SETD2 properties, and related mechanisms from the literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C68, C76-C77, and C90 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited. These provide necessary context for interpreting the current findings. The citations appear appropriate and accurately represent the cited work based on the claims made.

results.result: Speculative discussion of potential mechanisms by which H3K36 might affect gene expression, including effects on transcription elongation rate, recruitment of RNA modifying enzymes, contributions across multiple processing steps, and roles in 3D genome organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C83, C86-C89, and C91 are explicitly speculative, representing potential mechanisms and future directions rather than demonstrated findings. These are appropriately presented as possibilities requiring further investigation. While speculation is valuable for discussion, these claims cannot be evaluated as supported or unsupported by the current data.
